summary: Defines an X.509v3 certificate extension that lets a certificate say which TLS features a server must support. A main use is requiring OCSP stapling, so a client can fail immediately if a status response is not stapled, which prevents downgrade attacks that strip revocation checking.

plainLanguage.summary: A certificate can carry a note saying 'this website must always show its fresh safety check'. If the check is missing, the browser knows something is wrong.

questions: what is the tls feature extension in x.509
what is the tls feature extension
why does a missing ocsp staple matter
subtitle: A certificate extension that tells clients which TLS features the server must provide, so a missing OCSP staple means failure.

tldr.problem: A client cannot conclude anything from a missing OCSP stapled response, because the server may not support stapling or may be hiding the response on purpose because the certificate is invalid.
tldr.mechanism: The TLS feature extension is an X.509v3 certificate extension that lists TLS extension identifiers the server must support, such as status_request. A client that sees the feature listed can fail immediately when the server does not deliver it.
tldr.outcome: Clients no longer have to query the OCSP responder when the staple is absent, which removes a denial-of-service opening. The extension protects against downgrades only for certificates that carry it.

today: RFC 7633 is a Proposed Standard. The metadata for this RFC lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Problem With a Missing Staple
sections.content:
RFC 7633 is a Standards Track document. It defines a way to prevent downgrade attacks that the TLS protocol does not already prevent. The RFC says TLS itself protects strongly against most downgrades, including attacks on cipher suite choices and client credentials, so this extension is relevant only to validating TLS credentials.

The main case is revocation checking. With OCSP stapling (RFC 6066 and RFC 6961) a TLS server supplies proof of valid certificate status inside the handshake. That avoids the privacy, performance and reliability problems of making a third-party connection mid-handshake.

The weakness is the absent staple. A client cannot draw a conclusion from missing status information unless it knows the real server would have sent it. The server may simply not support stapling, or it may be withholding the response because it knows the certificate is invalid.
sections.plainLanguage: If a shop is supposed to show you a fresh safety certificate and it shows nothing, you cannot tell if it forgot or is hiding something. A note on the shop's licence saying 'must always show it' settles that.

sections.title: Two Meanings of Extension
sections.content:
Both X.509 and TLS use the word extension. To avoid confusion, this document reserves the term extension for X.509v3 certificate extensions. It uses TLS feature extension for what RFC 5246 calls an extension in the TLS protocol.

The only TLS features relevant to revocation status are status_request and status_request_v2 (Multiple Certificate Status). Both carry OCSP tokens in-band.
sections.plainLanguage: The same word means two different things here, like 'bat' for an animal and 'bat' for baseball. The RFC picks clear names so nobody mixes them up.

sections.title: The TLS Feature Extension
sections.content:
The extension is identified by id-pe-tlsfeature, defined as { id-pe 24 }. Its value is the DER encoding of Features ::= SEQUENCE OF INTEGER. Each integer is a TLS extension identifier taken from the IANA TLS Extensions registry.

The extension SHOULD NOT be marked critical. RFC 5280 requires implementations to reject certificates with critical extensions they do not understand, so marking it critical breaks backward compatibility unless that is the intent.

If the client requests one of the listed features in its ClientHello, the server MUST return a ServerHello that satisfies the request. A server offering a certificate with this extension MUST support the listed features. The RFC does not require a client to offer or support any feature, whether or not the certificate lists it.
sections.plainLanguage: The note is just a list of feature numbers written in the certificate. The server promises to support everything on the list.

sections.title: Where It Is Used and Who Does What
sections.content:
The extension can appear in three places. In a PKCS #10 Certificate Signing Request (RFC 2986) it may be given as a CSR attribute, so a server can tell the Certification Authority (CA) what it supports. In a CA certificate (key usage keyCertSign) it constrains chains: a certificate signed by such a CA MUST carry the same set of features or a superset. In a server end-entity certificate (EKU id-kp-serverAuth) it states what the server MUST provide.

A CA SHOULD NOT issue the extension unless the end entity has said it intends to support the features, and SHOULD make sure OCSP tokens are published before the certificate is released. A server SHOULD verify its configuration matches the certificate, and SHOULD NOT start using a replacement certificate until the needed OCSP tokens are available.

A client MUST treat the certificate as invalid if the server's features do not include everything present in both the ClientHello and the extension. If valid TLS is mandated by policy or the application protocol, the client MUST refuse the connection. Otherwise it MAY continue but MUST NOT treat the certificate as valid.
sections.plainLanguage: The shop asks for the note, the licence office only adds it if the shop can really do it, and the visitor leaves if the shop breaks the promise.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Using the extension is optional, and it is a post-issue control. It helps when a certificate carrying the feature is compromised after issue. It does not help when an attacker obtains an unmarked certificate from an issuer through fraud, which needs controls that act before issue, such as CAA records (RFC 6844).

A CA could issue a certificate demanding a feature it knows the server cannot support. The RFC judges the consequences limited, since the CA could equally refuse to issue the certificate. The extension also gives no protection against cipher suite downgrade, which is left to TLS itself.
sections.plainLanguage: The note only helps for certificates that carry it. A crook with a plain certificate with no note is not stopped by this.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA added id-pe-tlsfeature as decimal 24 in the SMI Security for PKIX Certificate Extension registry (1.3.6.1.5.5.7.1). It also added id-mod-tls-feature-2015 as decimal 86 in the PKIX Module Identifier registry (1.3.6.1.5.5.7.0). Appendix A gives the ASN.1 module.
sections.plainLanguage: The official list of numbers got two new entries so everyone uses the same number for this note.

data.title: ASN.1 definition
data.code:
id-pe-tlsfeature OBJECT IDENTIFIER ::=  { id-pe 24 }

Features ::= SEQUENCE OF INTEGER
